overview:
For most of its first few centuries the place was unremarkable — a modest town on a branch of the Euphrates in central Mesopotamia, mentioned in passing in records of the Akkadian and Ur III states in the late third millennium BCE. Its rise began around 1894 BCE, when an Amorite dynasty took control, and became decisive under Hammurabi (roughly 1792–1750 BCE), who absorbed Isin, Larsa and Eshnunna and left the long law collection that still carries his name. That empire fragmented soon after his death; a Hittite raid struck the city in 1595 BCE, and Kassite kings then ruled from it for some four centuries, long enough that "Babylonia" became the standard name for southern Mesopotamia. The city's later career was one of repeated humiliation and recovery under Assyrian domination, culminating in 689 BCE when Sennacherib, exasperated by revolt, had Babylon sacked and deliberately wrecked — an act his successors partly undid by rebuilding it.

The version everyone pictures belongs to the Neo-Babylonian century after 626 BCE, and above all to Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BCE), who rebuilt on a scale of roughly 900 hectares behind concentric walls, laid out the Processional Way, faced the Ishtar Gate in glazed blue brick with striding lions, bulls and dragons, and raised the ziggurat Etemenanki that later readers folded into the Tower of Babel story. This is also the Babylon of the Judahite deportations, which is why so much of its reputation reaches us through the Hebrew Bible, written by people it had conquered. Cyrus the Great took the city in 539 BCE and it became a Persian administrative centre rather than an imperial capital; Alexander entered it in 331 BCE, planned to restore it, and died there in 323. The founding of Seleucia on the Tigris drew away population and administration, and though Babylon was never simply abandoned — its temple scribes were still compiling astronomical diaries and almanacs into the first century CE, the last stream of cuneiform writing anywhere — by the turn of the era it was a shrunken religious and scholarly town beside its own ruins.

What can actually be seen and studied is uneven. Robert Koldewey's German excavations from 1899 to 1914 exposed the Neo-Babylonian city in detail and shipped the Ishtar Gate's brickwork to Berlin, where it was reassembled in the Pergamon Museum — an acquisition made under late Ottoman permissions that is now contested. Koldewey worked during a period of unusually low groundwater and reached levels that have since gone under; barrage construction upstream raised the water table, and Hammurabi's own city lies largely beneath it, effectively unexcavatable. The modern site has suffered further: Saddam Hussein built a palace overlooking it and reconstructed walls on ancient foundations with bricks stamped in his own name, and after 2003 a coalition military base was installed among the ruins, causing damage that UNESCO documented in detail. Babylon was inscribed as a World Heritage site only in 2019.
significance: Babylon supplied the ancient Near East with a template for what a capital could be — a city whose prestige outlasted every dynasty that held it, so that Assyrian, Persian and Macedonian conquerors all found it worth possessing and repairing rather than erasing. Its scribal schools transmitted Sumerian and Akkadian literature for well over a millennium, and its temple astronomers compiled the longest continuous run of dated observations in human history, records that Greek astronomers drew on and that modern scientists still use to track changes in the Earth's rotation. Through the Hebrew Bible and Greek writers it also became a symbol rather than a place — of imperial arrogance, of exile, of the confusion of tongues — a second life that has shaped how it is imagined far more than any excavation report, and that still tangles with the archaeology of the actual mound in Iraq.
coverage: Written from reference and institutional overviews of the site and its excavation history; the dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped point. The record itself is lopsided: the Neo-Babylonian city is well documented and well excavated, while Hammurabi's Babylon is physically inaccessible under the water table and known mainly from texts found elsewhere, and much of the city's popular reputation comes from hostile or second-hand sources — biblical authors writing as deportees, and Greek writers like Herodotus reporting on a city they may not have seen. The Hanging Gardens have never been located at Babylon and may not have been there.
